# Childhood & adolescence

> *Between early childhood and adulthood the body grows for a decade and lays down most of its adult
> bone, while children form eating habits that tend to persist. We cover the internal changes (growth, bone and
> iron), the external influences (the food environment, peers and sport), and how to recognise trouble
> without causing harm, since careless talk about weight can do damage at this age.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain why nutritional demand in the growth spurt tracks pubertal stage, not age, and why energy and
  protein needs fall per kilogram while total needs rise.
- Explain why peak bone mass acquisition in adolescence matters for later life, which factors
  (weight-bearing activity, calcium, vitamin D, adequate energy) change bone accrual, and how strong the
  evidence is for each.
- Explain why the menstruating adolescent girl is the classic group at risk of iron deficiency, and why
  ferritin detects deficiency before anaemia.
- Evaluate the evidence that sugary drinks, food marketing, screen time and family meals shape adolescent
  eating and weight.
- Recognise low energy availability and the female-athlete triad in a young athlete, and refer.
- Explain why dieting and weight-talk harm adolescents, and recognise the eating-disorder red flags, at
  any weight, that warrant referral.
:::

## Childhood & adolescence at a glance: internal and external factors {#sec-overview}

This stage runs from about age 4 or 5, once a child eats family foods, to the end of adolescence (for the
earlier years, see the [*Infancy & early childhood*](infancy-early-childhood.qmd) chapter). The period has
two phases: a long school-age phase (about 5–10 years) of steady growth in which habits set, and a
short adolescent growth spurt. As at every life stage, two sets of factors shape nutrition:

| Factor | What changes at this stage |
|---|---|
| Internal factors (inside the body) | After years of slow, steady growth, the growth spurt re-accelerates height, and sex hormones make body composition diverge by sex. The window for accruing peak bone mass opens briefly and then closes for good. Iron demand rises with growth and, in girls, jumps again once menstruation begins. |
| External factors (life and environment) | The school and hawker food environment, sugary drinks and their marketing, physical activity and sport, and the handover of food choice from parent to teenager and peers. |

## What changes inside: growth, bone and iron {#sec-child-inside}

The growth spurt drives the internal changes of this stage: it sets energy and protein needs, opens the brief window for peak bone mass, and, with menstruation in girls, raises the demand for iron.

### The growth spurt: timing, energy and protein {#sec-child-growth}

After infancy, growth is slow and steady for years; puberty then re-accelerates it to a **peak height
velocity**, the fastest growth since the first year of life [@rogol_2000_growth_puberty]. Because the
spurt is transient and timed by pubertal stage, not birthday, a child's height is best interpreted as a point on
a velocity curve.

The spurt comes early in girls and late in boys. A girl's fastest growth comes in early puberty, before
**menarche** (the first menstrual period), so she is at or near peak nutritional demand while still
looking like a child. A boy's biggest spurt comes later, so a boy just entering puberty still has his
ahead of him [@granados_2015_phv_tanner]. Sex hormones then make body composition diverge: testosterone
builds lean mass in boys, and oestrogen adds body fat in girls. This divergence is normal, hormone-driven
physiology, not over-eating, and needs no correction [@rogol_2000_growth_puberty].

Energy and protein needs rise in total but fall per kilogram. Total daily energy needs climb steeply and
diverge by sex: a late-teen boy may need close to double a young child's intake. Per kilogram, however,
energy needs fall through childhood, mainly because a bigger body burns less energy per kilogram at rest
[@faowhounu_2004_energy_children]. Protein behaves the same way: the requirement per kilogram drifts down
toward the adult figure, while total grams rise because the teenager is bigger
[@faowhounu_protein_children]. An ordinary diet that meets energy needs therefore almost always meets
protein needs too, so a teenager who eats normally rarely needs protein powder. (Reference intakes and the underlying nutrient biology are in the [*Macronutrients*](macronutrients.qmd) and [*Micronutrients, hydration and electrolytes*](04-micronutrients-hydration.qmd) chapters.)

A teenager's large appetite mostly reflects the bigger body and more movement. The direct energy cost of
laying down new tissue is small, about 1–2% of the day's energy by mid-adolescence
[@faowhounu_2004_energy_children]. The appetite surge is a normal, hormonally coordinated signal that
tracks growth velocity [@cheng_2018_ghrelin_puberty], so appetite is best judged against growth. A
mid-pubertal teenager eating far more is usually meeting the needs of a growth spurt. The warning sign is intake that
does not fit the growth trajectory: restriction while the growth curve falters, or rapid fat gain.

The capacity for **catch-up growth** (recovering growth lost after a nutritional setback) narrows with
age. A young child can recover from a setback, but by later childhood that potential shrinks, so a child
crossing down through the growth centiles (the reference curves on a growth chart) warrants referral, not
watchful waiting [@leroy_2020_catchup_growth].

### Peak bone mass acquisition {#sec-child-bone}

Bone is not laid down evenly across life. Roughly two-fifths of the bone mineral an adult carries is
deposited in the few years around the growth spurt, a brief, hormone-dependent window that then closes as the
growth plates fuse [@baxterjones_2011_pbm_estimation]. The bone mass accrued by the end of adolescence,
close to a person's **peak bone mass** (the most bone a person ever has), is a major
determinant of how much bone loss a person can tolerate in later life (see the
[*Bone & joint health*](bone-health-osteoporosis.qmd) and
[*Menopause & midlife health*](menopause-midlife.qmd) chapters). The window is only partly
modifiable: lifestyle sets about a fifth to two-fifths of peak bone mass, and the rest is inherited
[@nof_weaver_2016_pbm_position]. Lifestyle is worth improving, but it does not override genetics.

The interactive below pictures peak bone mass as a "bone bank" filled during this window. Move the age
slider to watch accrual climb steeply and then plateau, toggle the lifestyle factors to see how far they move
the attainable peak within the shaded band, and switch on the under-fuelling threat to see that peak fall.

<div data-island="bone-window" data-src="/diagrams/bone-window.yml"></div>

What builds bone is more specific, and more complicated, than the advice to "drink milk". The strongest evidence for
building peak bone mass is for weight-bearing, high-impact activity and adequate calcium; dairy and
vitamin D help but the evidence for them is weaker [@nof_weaver_2016_pbm_position].
Exercise is most **osteogenic** (bone-building) in early puberty, when the window is widest
[@hind_2007_exercise_bone_review].

The evidence on supplements is easily misread. In a child who is already replete, calcium supplements add
only a small, fading benefit and vitamin D supplements add essentially nothing; the gains show up only in
children who were deficient to begin with [@winzenberg_2006_calcium_meta; @winzenberg_2011_vitd_meta].
The message is therefore food-first calcium, outdoor weight-bearing activity, and finding and treating
deficiency, not blanket supplementation.

::: {.callout-warning}
## When bone accrual is under threat: often energy, not calcium
In adolescence, bone accrual is often impaired by too little energy. In a teenager who trains hard
and eats too little, reproductive hormone (oestrogen) production falls, menstrual periods stop
(**amenorrhoea**) and bone accrual stalls, sometimes with a lasting deficit
[@ackerman_2011_athlete_bone_triad]. **A young athlete with irregular periods, amenorrhoea or a stress
fracture is at risk of lasting bone loss: recognise it and refer, and do not reach for a calcium
tablet.** We return to this pattern under [Sport and energy availability](#sec-child-sport).
:::

### Iron and the menstruating adolescent {#sec-child-iron}

Iron demand rises through childhood, in both sexes during the spurt, to build an expanding blood volume
and growing muscle. In girls it jumps again at menarche, as monthly menstrual loss adds to the demand of
growth [@beard_2000_iron_adolescent_females]. The menstruating adolescent girl is therefore the classic
at-risk group, and the risk rises further when heavy periods occur with a diet low in meat, a combination that
multiplies the odds of deficiency compared with either factor alone [@soderman_2025_menstrual_iron]. Singapore's
recommendations reflect this: the iron recommendation for adolescent girls is roughly triple that for
their pre-teen years, and far above boys' [@hpb_healthhub_rda].

Iron deficiency matters beyond a low haemoglobin. It blunts attention, memory and learning, and correcting
it measurably improves them, though without a clear effect on exam results [@gutema_2023_iron_cognition].
Deficiency also develops before anaemia: an iron-depleted teenager can be tired and under-performing with
a normal haemoglobin. For that reason **ferritin**, a marker of iron status that falls before haemoglobin
does, matters more than haemoglobin alone. When you see a tired, poorly concentrating or heavily
menstruating adolescent, especially one on a meat-restricted diet, suspect iron deficiency and check iron
studies (blood tests of iron status, including ferritin) or refer, without waiting for anaemia. (Exact
thresholds and screening schedules belong to clinical practice; iron deficiency and anaemia are covered in
the *Micronutrients, hydration and electrolytes* chapter.)

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Getting iron from everyday meals
The practical gains come from combining foods, not from supplements. Haem iron (in meat, fish and poultry)
is far better absorbed than the non-haem iron of plants, and a little meat or a food rich in vitamin C (a
squeeze of lime, some vegetables, fruit after the meal) can multiply absorption from a plate of rice or
noodles [@statpearls_dietary_iron; @nih_ods_iron_hp]. The common blockers are tea and coffee with meals,
the after-school *teh* or *kopi*, and calcium taken at the same time, so move those between meals, away
from the iron-rich one. A vegetarian teenager needs noticeably more dietary iron and is worth asking about
directly [@nih_ods_iron_hp].
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a 13-year-old boy suddenly eats far more than he used to. Why is this usually normal, and what would make it a concern?
The appetite surge of puberty is a normal, hormonally coordinated signal that tracks growth velocity. The
extra intake mostly reflects his bigger body and more movement; laying down new tissue itself costs only
about 1–2% of the day's energy. Because appetite tracks growth, intake that fits his growth
trajectory usually reflects a growth spurt. Restriction while his growth curve falters, or rapid fat gain,
would be the warning sign.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does bone accrual missed at 14 still matter in later life?
Roughly two-fifths of adult bone mineral is laid down in the few years around the growth spurt, and the
window closes as the growth plates fuse, so a shortfall in those years can leave a lasting deficit. The
bone mass accrued by the end of adolescence is a major determinant of how much bone loss a person can tolerate in later life. Lifestyle sets only about a fifth to two-fifths of peak bone mass, but that
share is worth protecting.
:::

## What changes outside: environment, peers and sport {#sec-child-outside}

The external influences on adolescent eating range from the food environment (sugary drinks, marketing, screens and family meals) to sport, where the danger is eating too little for the training load.

### Sugary drinks, food marketing and peer influence {#sec-child-environment}

In adolescence, food choice moves from the parent to the teenager and their peers. Teenagers eat more
meals out, skip more meals and meet more advertising, and the family meal weakens as an influence just as
sugary drinks and marketing gain strength [@story2002adolescent]. Two environmental influences stand out.

**Free sugars and sugary drinks.** The WHO ceiling of free sugars under 10% of energy, and better under
5%, is based first on dental caries (tooth decay), not weight [@who2015sugars]. On weight, the
strongest evidence comes from trials that swapped sugary for sugar-free drinks. A double-blind trial in
children found less weight gain over 18 months, and an open-label trial in adolescents saw a benefit that
had faded by 2 years [@deruyter2012ssb; @ebbeling2012ssb]. The effect is real but modest, and it works
mostly through the drinks' energy content, not through any unique toxicity of sugar
[@temorenga2012sugars]. Sugary drinks are a risk to recognise at this life stage, not a toxin to
fear.

**Marketing and screens.** Food advertising measurably shifts what children eat and ask for
[@boyland2016adcue; @boyland2022marketing], enough that the WHO now calls for mandatory limits on
marketing unhealthy food to under-18s [@who2023marketing]. Screen time is associated with heavier weight,
but the link runs both ways: heavier children may also choose more sedentary screen time. Much of the
effect also runs through other pathways (eating while watching, exposure to the adverts and lost sleep), so
screen time is one of several interlinked influences, not a single cause [@zhang2016tvobesity;
@robinson2017screenmedia].

Family meals can offset some of these influences. Eating together several times a week is associated with better diets,
healthier weight and less disordered eating. The association is largely observational and plausibly runs
both ways, so family meals are encouraged as a low-risk, sensible habit, not prescribed as a treatment
[@hammons2011familymeals; @berge2015familymeals].

### Sport and energy availability {#sec-child-sport}

The starting point for every adolescent is enough activity. The guideline is an average of at least
60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity, plus muscle- and bone-strengthening activity on 3 days
a week, a target most Singaporean teenagers miss [@bull2020whopa; @sg24hrGuidelines2021].

The danger at the other end is under-fuelling: an active adolescent needs enough energy, not weight loss.
Three terms describe the risk:

Energy availability
: The energy left for the body's other physiological functions after the energy cost of training: intake
  minus the energy burned in exercise.

Female-athlete triad
: The linked trio of low energy availability, menstrual disturbance and impaired bone health.

Relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs)
: The broader form of the female-athlete triad, arising from low energy availability.

When energy availability stays too low for too long, from dieting, disordered eating or simply not
matching a heavy training load, hormone production (including oestrogen) is suppressed: amenorrhoea
develops, bone accrual stalls and performance falls. The female-athlete triad and its broader form,
relative energy deficiency in sport, name this cluster [@mountjoy2023reds; @weisskelly2016triad].

::: {.flow}
[Under-fuelling in sport]{.tree-title}

1. Intake falls short of training
2. Energy availability stays low
3. Hormone production falls (including oestrogen)
4. Periods stop; bone and performance suffer
:::

Sports medicine's rule of thumb is that adequate energy is the foundation, and that one part of the triad
should prompt a look for the others [@thomas2016nutritionathletic]. An under-fuelled adolescent with
amenorrhoea or a stress fracture therefore needs recognition and referral, not a stricter diet. (Sports
nutrition in more detail is in the [*Adulthood*](adulthood-working-life.qmd) chapter.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: teenagers who share family meals have better diets. Why are family meals encouraged but not prescribed as a treatment?
The association is largely observational and plausibly runs both ways, so it does not show that family
meals cause the better diets. Because family meals are low-risk and sensible, they are still encouraged
as a habit, and they help offset peer influence and marketing as food choice passes to the teenager.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a 16-year-old runner eats ordinary meals but trains twice a day, and her periods have stopped. How can she be under-fuelled?
Energy availability is intake minus the energy burned in exercise, so ordinary meals can leave too little
for the body's other physiological functions when the training load is heavy. When energy availability
stays low, hormone production (including oestrogen) falls: amenorrhoea develops, bone accrual stalls and
performance falls.
One part of the triad should prompt a look for the others, and she needs recognition and referral, not
a stricter diet.
:::

## Recognising trouble, and when to refer {#sec-child-refer}

Two clinical problems emerge in adolescence (disordered eating and obesity), and the same messages
prevent both.

**Disordered eating.** Adolescence is the peak age of onset for eating disorders: anorexia nervosa,
bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder typically begin in the early teens
[@swanson_2011_ncsa_ed_adolescents].

Anorexia nervosa
: Restriction of energy intake that leads to a low body weight, with an intense fear of gaining weight.

Bulimia nervosa
: Recurrent binge eating (an unusually large amount of food in a short time, with a sense of loss of
  control), followed by compensation such as vomiting, fasting or excessive exercise.

Binge-eating disorder
: Recurrent binge eating (an unusually large amount of food in a short time, with a sense of loss of
  control) without regular compensation such as vomiting or fasting.

Dieting is not a harmless habit in adolescence. In prospective studies, adolescents who diet are far more
likely than non-dieters to develop a new eating disorder and, paradoxically, to gain more weight over the
following years [@patton_1999_adolescent_ed_onset; @neumarksztainer_2007_dieting_weightgain_eat2]. That
single finding links both problems.

Two points help with recognition. First, eating disorders occur across the whole weight spectrum: a
formerly heavier teenager who loses weight fast can be seriously ill, so praising weight loss can mask an
emerging disorder [@chew_2023_atypical_an_sg_adolescents]. Second, the red flags are concrete; they are
worth checking at every routine visit, and any one of them warrants referral
[@hornberger_2021_aap_identify_ed]:

- Faltering or crossing-down growth
- A marked or rapid weight change
- Amenorrhoea
- A stress fracture
- Purging or highly restrictive eating

Two further patterns are worth recognising. **Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID)** is
restrictive eating driven by sensory aversion or fear, without concern about weight or shape. It is where
"fussy eating" becomes clinical (see the *Infancy & early childhood* chapter)
[@sanchez_arfid_2023_epi_review]. **Orthorexia**, an obsessive fixation on "clean eating", is a real
pattern, fuelled by social media, that is worth recognising even though it is not yet a formal diagnosis
[@horovitz_orthorexia_2023_review].

**Obesity and emerging type 2 diabetes.** Adolescence is a high-risk window for weight gain partly
because the physiology of puberty coincides with an obesogenic environment. Per-kilogram energy needs are falling, and a
transient insulin resistance (the body's cells responding less to insulin, so the pancreas makes more to
keep blood glucose normal) is a normal part of puberty. A healthy pubertal teenager carrying a little more
fat is therefore usually showing physiology, not disease, and should not be pathologised.

The concern is the trajectory. Childhood obesity tends to track into adulthood, and paediatric type 2
diabetes is now emerging as a consequence, including in Singapore [@singh_2008_tracking_overweight;
@nuh_paediatric_t2dm_children]. Here too the task is to recognise the trajectory and its cardiometabolic
risk, and refer (management is in the [*Obesity & metabolic syndrome*](obesity-metabolic-syndrome.qmd)
and [*Type 2 diabetes*](type-2-diabetes.qmd) chapters).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do no harm: healthy habits, never a diet
Because dieting predicts both a new eating disorder and more weight gain, the same safe approach serves
both problems. Paediatric guidance recommends the same: focus on healthy habits rather than weight, encourage family
meals, and avoid all weight-talk and teasing, which drive disordered eating
[@golden_2016_aap_prevent_obesity_ed; @haines_2006_weight_teasing_eat]. **Whatever a teenager's weight,
the answer is never "go on a diet".** How to raise the subject of weight safely is
taught in the [*Assessing diet and talking to patients*](06-dietary-assessment.qmd) chapter; the task here
is to recognise and refer.
:::

Across this stage, any of the following warrants referral:

- Growth faltering or crossing down the centiles
- Suspected iron deficiency (tiredness, poor concentration, heavy periods, a meat-restricted diet)
- The under-fuelled athlete (amenorrhoea, a stress or recurrent fracture, dropping performance)
- Any eating-disorder red flag above, at any weight, including rapid weight loss in a formerly heavier teenager
- Obesity on a cardiometabolic trajectory

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does one message, healthy habits and never a diet, protect against both disordered eating and obesity?
In prospective studies, adolescents who diet are far more likely than non-dieters to develop a new eating
disorder, and are also more likely to gain more weight over the following years. Dieting therefore
predicts both a new eating disorder and more weight gain (the path to obesity), so the same safe
approach (healthy habits, family meals, no weight-talk or teasing) serves both.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a healthy 13-year-old girl in puberty has gained a little fat. Why is this usually not disease, and what would change that?
In puberty oestrogen adds body fat in girls, and a transient insulin resistance is normal. A little extra
fat in a healthy pubertal girl is therefore usually physiology, not over-eating, and should not be
pathologised. The concern is the trajectory: childhood obesity tends to track into
adulthood, and paediatric type 2 diabetes is emerging as a consequence. A trajectory with cardiometabolic
risk warrants recognition and referral, never a diet.
:::

## Is adolescence just "feed them more"? {#sec-close}

Feeding teenagers more is not enough: the internal factors of this stage set needs for quality and timing, not sheer quantity, and getting those needs wrong can cause harm. The spurt needs enough energy and iron (the menstruating girl is the one to watch),
and bone accrual needs enough weight-bearing activity and calcium before its window largely closes by
the early twenties. Because dieting and weight-talk can start real disease, the safe approach to any
teenager's weight is healthy habits, never a diet, together with knowing the red flags that mean it is
time to refer.

## The Singapore context {#sec-singapore}

**School food, and a cautionary tale.** The Healthy Meals in Schools Programme shapes the food a
Singaporean student meets daily. Participating canteens must cut fat, sugar and salt, serve wholegrains
and vegetables, keep plain water the default, and discourage sugary drinks [@hpb_hmsp_page].

Singapore's earlier school anti-obesity scheme, TAF ("Trim And Fit", ~1992–2007), did reduce measured
childhood obesity. It is nonetheless Singapore's best-known example of how not to run such a scheme:
heavier children were singled out and teased (the acronym reads "FAT" backwards). It was retired in 2007
for a whole-school Holistic Health Framework that does not stigmatise [@foo2013_sg_obesity]. A local
follow-up of anorexia-nervosa patients found that about one in ten had been through TAF before their
illness began, an association, not proof of cause [@kuek_2015_an_singapore]. The lesson is the
do-no-harm rule, now national policy: weight is screened without shaming the child.

**Sugary drinks and drink labelling.** Nutri-Grade, the mandatory A–D drink label with an advertising
ban on the worst grade, was designed for exactly the drinks teenagers buy. Since December 2023 it has
also covered freshly prepared beverages, bubble tea included [@hpbNutriGrade; @mohNutriGradeFresh2023].
Its effect is modest: a small cut in sugar per serving [@shin2023_nutrigrade_rct]. Local data also show
that most children already exceed added-sugar guidance [@brownlee2019sgchildren], so the label is one
measure among many, best combined with changes at home and at school.

**A vitamin D tension, and a data gap.** Singapore's recommendations track these physiological changes well: iron rises
steeply for adolescent girls (see [Iron and the menstruating adolescent](#sec-child-iron)) and calcium
stays high through the bone-building years, but vitamin D is set unusually low, on the assumption of
abundant tropical sun [@hpb_healthhub_rda]. That assumption sits awkwardly with regional evidence that
vitamin D insufficiency is common despite the sun, because of indoor, sun-avoidant, screen-heavy
lifestyles [@nimitphong_2013_vitd_sea]. Direct Singapore data on adolescent
iron and vitamin D status are sparse, so some of the evidence here is regional or international.

**Activity and eating disorders locally.** Only about a quarter of older teens meet the daily activity
target [@tay2023sgreportcard]. Too little physical activity is one of the habits targeted by Grow Well SG,
a whole-of-government strategy launched in 2025 that starts with children up to 12 [@moh_growwellsg].
Eating disorders are neither rare nor imported. Local surveys find a meaningful fraction of schoolgirls
screen positive for risk (with Malay girls over-represented), presentations are rising and diagnosed younger, and a
large share are atypical, non-underweight presentations [@ho2006_sg_eating_risk; @wong2022_paed_ed;
@chew_2023_atypical_an_sg_adolescents]. These atypical presentations show that, in Singapore too, eating
disorders occur across the weight spectrum.
